pages.question: A 45-year-old man with obesity (BMI 38 kg/m²), hypertriglyceridemia, and a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma in his father presents requesting tirzepatide for weight loss. He read about the medication online and is enthusiastic about starting it. He has no prior pharmacotherapy for obesity. His current medications include fenofibrate and fish oil. He denies nausea, abdominal pain, or prior episodes of pancreatitis. Serum lipase and amylase are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient's request?

answers.text: Initiate tirzepatide since only personal history of medullary thyroid carcinoma is a contraindication
Initiate tirzepatide with serum calcitonin monitoring every 6 months
Initiate semaglutide instead, as it does not carry thyroid C-cell tumor risk
Order a serum calcitonin level and proceed with tirzepatide if it is normal
Decline tirzepatide and counsel the patient that his family history is a contraindication to this drug class

pages.question: A 45-year-old man with obesity (BMI 38 kg/m²), hypertriglyceridemia, and a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma in his father presents requesting tirzepatide for weight loss. He read about the medication online and is enthusiastic about starting it. He has no prior pharmacotherapy for obesity. His current medications include fenofibrate and fish oil. He denies nausea, abdominal pain, or prior episodes of pancreatitis. Serum lipase and amylase are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate response to this patient's request?

answers.text:
Initiate tirzepatide since only personal history of medullary thyroid carcinoma is a contraindication
(25%)

Initiate tirzepatide with serum calcitonin monitoring every 6 months
(50%)

Initiate semaglutide instead, as it does not carry thyroid C-cell tumor risk
(0%)

Order a serum calcitonin level and proceed with tirzepatide if it is normal
(0%)

Decline tirzepatide and counsel the patient that his family history is a contraindication to this drug class
(25%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
A personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 is an absolute contraindication to GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists including tirzepatide, due to the risk of thyroid C-cell tumor development demonstrated in rodent studies. The familial nature of medullary thyroid carcinoma — particularly in the context of MEN2 — necessitates avoidance of this drug class even when the patient himself is unaffected. Alternative antiobesity pharmacotherapy should be selected after excluding this contraindication.
(Choice A)
Initiate tirzepatide since only personal history of medullary thyroid carcinoma is a contraindication
This is incorrect. Both personal AND family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 are absolute contraindications to tirzepatide and all GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists per FDA labeling. A family history raises concern for hereditary MTC associated with MEN2 and RET mutations, which could place the patient himself at elevated thyroid C-cell risk. Prescribing tirzepatide in this setting would violate the labeled contraindication.
(Choice B)
Initiate tirzepatide with serum calcitonin monitoring every 6 months
While serum calcitonin monitoring has been proposed as a surveillance strategy for thyroid C-cell changes in patients on GLP-1/GIP agonists, a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma is an absolute contraindication to tirzepatide per FDA labeling. The contraindication exists because animal studies demonstrated dose-dependent thyroid C-cell hyperplasia and tumors in rodents. Monitoring calcitonin does not mitigate this underlying contraindication.
(Choice C)
Initiate semaglutide instead, as it does not carry thyroid C-cell tumor risk
Semaglutide is also a GLP-1 receptor agonist and carries the same class contraindication regarding personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2. The thyroid C-cell tumor risk is a class effect of GLP-1 receptor agonists, not unique to tirzepatide. Substituting semaglutide does not circumvent the contraindication and would be equally inappropriate in this patient.
(Choice D)
Order a serum calcitonin level and proceed with tirzepatide if it is normal
A normal baseline calcitonin level does not rule out future thyroid C-cell tumor risk with GLP-1/GIP agonist exposure and does not override the FDA contraindication for family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma. The contraindication is based on precautionary principles from animal studies showing thyroid C-cell tumors, not on baseline calcitonin levels. Testing calcitonin does not change the inappropriateness of prescribing tirzepatide in this patient.
(Choice E)
Decline tirzepatide and counsel the patient that his family history is a contraindication to this drug class
Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist FDA-approved for chronic weight management in adults with BMI ≥30 or ≥27 with weight-related comorbidities. However, a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) is an absolute contraindication to tirzepatide and all GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists, because animal studies demonstrated dose-dependent thyroid C-cell hyperplasia and tumors in rodents exposed to these agents. The risk to humans is uncertain but the precautionary contraindication applies to both personal and family history of MTC or MEN2. The patient's father's MTC may indicate a hereditary MEN2 syndrome with RET proto-oncogene mutation, placing this patient at elevated thyroid C-cell risk. This patient should be counseled clearly about the contraindication, referred for genetic evaluation if appropriate, and offered an alternative antiobesity medication such as naltrexone-bupropion or orlistat pending further evaluation. Lifestyle and dietary counseling should continue in parallel.

pages.question: A 55-year-old woman with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections presents to the clinic with complaints of bilateral hearing difficulty and unsteadiness while walking. She reports that over the past two weeks, she has noticed trouble understanding conversations in noisy environments and a sensation of spinning when she turns her head quickly. She denies vertigo at rest but notes increased imbalance in the dark. Two months ago, she was treated with intravenous amikacin for a multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli pyelonephritis. Audiometric testing reveals bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. Vestibular testing shows reduced caloric responses bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient, recently treated with amikacin, presents with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular symptoms consistent with aminoglycoside ototoxicity affecting both the cochlea and vestibular system. Key features include high-frequency hearing loss, imbalance worsened in the dark, and abnormal vestibular tests. Other diagnoses are less likely given the temporal association with aminoglycoside use and bilateral symmetric findings.
(Choice A)
Meniere disease
Meniere disease involves episodic vertigo with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, typically unilateral. The bilateral symmetric hearing loss and clear temporal relationship with amikacin treatment are inconsistent with this diagnosis.
(Choice B)
Aminoglycoside ototoxicity
Aminoglycosides like amikacin can cause bilateral cochlear (sensorineural hearing loss) and vestibular toxicity (imbalance, abnormal vestibular tests), matching the patient's presentation and treatment history.
(Choice C)
Cerebellar stroke
Cerebellar stroke may cause imbalance and vertigo, but typically presents acutely with additional signs like dysmetria or ataxia, and lacks hearing loss or medication-related etiology.
(Choice D)
Unilateral acoustic neuroma
Acoustic neuroma typically presents with unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance. The bilateral symmetric presentation and temporal association with aminoglycoside treatment make this diagnosis unlikely.
(Choice E)
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
BPPV causes brief episodes of vertigo triggered by specific head movements without hearing loss. This patient has persistent bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular dysfunction temporally related to aminoglycoside exposure.

pages.question: A 68-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation is admitted for elective hip replacement surgery. Postoperatively, she is started on unfractionated heparin for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis. On postoperative day 7, her platelet count decreases from a baseline of 280,000/mm³ to 120,000/mm³, and she develops acute shortness of breath with imaging confirming a new pulmonary embolism. Laboratory testing shows a positive heparin-PF4 antibody. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text:
Switch to low-molecular-weight heparin and monitor platelet count
(5.06%)

Continue unfractionated heparin and administer platelet transfusions
(0%)

Stop all heparin products and initiate argatroban
(84.81%)

Stop anticoagulation and observe with serial platelet counts
(2.53%)

Stop heparin and immediately start warfarin without bridging anticoagulation
(7.59%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
Suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) in a patient with >50% platelet count drop 7 days after heparin initiation and new thrombosis; requires stopping heparin and starting nonheparin anticoagulation immediately.
(Choice A)
Switch to low-molecular-weight heparin and monitor platelet count
This is incorrect; LMWH contains heparin and exhibits significant cross-reactivity with heparin-PF4 antibodies in approximately 90% of HIT cases, making it unsuitable as an alternative anticoagulant.
(Choice B)
Continue unfractionated heparin and administer platelet transfusions
This is incorrect; continuing heparin will perpetuate the immune-mediated platelet activation and thrombosis risk in HIT. Additionally, platelet transfusions are contraindicated in HIT as they can paradoxically increase thrombosis risk by providing more platelets for activation.
(Choice C)
Stop all heparin products and initiate argatroban
This is correct; suspected HIT requires immediate cessation of all heparin and starting a nonheparin anticoagulant like argatroban to prevent further thrombosis.
(Choice D)
Stop anticoagulation and observe with serial platelet counts
This is incorrect; HIT creates a paradoxical hypercoagulable state despite thrombocytopenia. Stopping anticoagulation without alternative therapy leaves the patient at extremely high risk for arterial and venous thrombosis, as evidenced by this patient's new pulmonary embolism.
(Choice E)
Stop heparin and immediately start warfarin without bridging anticoagulation
This is incorrect; warfarin monotherapy without bridging anticoagulation can cause warfarin-induced skin necrosis due to transient hypercoagulability from protein C depletion. Warfarin should only be initiated after platelet recovery (>150,000/mm³) and with concurrent nonheparin anticoagulation.

pages.question: A 35-year-old woman is admitted to the burn unit after suffering extensive scald burns from hot oil, affecting approximately 45% of her total body surface area, primarily on her torso and lower extremities. She presents with a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg, a heart rate of 130 beats/min, and decreased urine output, consistent with hypovolemic shock. Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation is required to restore intravascular volume. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial fluid choice for her resuscitation?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
Severe scald burns cause significant intravascular volume depletion due to fluid loss and capillary leakage, leading to hypovolemic shock. Lactated Ringer solution is the preferred isotonic crystalloid for resuscitation as it is balanced, contains electrolytes close to physiologic levels, and includes lactate as a buffer to help mitigate acidosis. Normal saline can lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Hypotonic solutions like 5% dextrose or half-normal saline risk causing hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Colloid solutions like albumin are not recommended for initial burn resuscitation due to lack of proven benefit over crystalloids and potential risks.
(Choice A)
5% Albumin
Colloid solutions like albumin are not recommended for initial burn resuscitation. The SAFE study and subsequent meta-analyses show no mortality benefit over crystalloids, while albumin is significantly more expensive. Additionally, increased capillary permeability from burn injury allows albumin to leak into the interstitium, reducing its intravascular volume expansion effect.
(Choice B)
5% Dextrose in water
5% dextrose in water is a hypotonic solution that provides free water without adequate sodium replacement. When infused rapidly for hypovolemic shock, it can lead to hyponatremia and cerebral edema as the dextrose is quickly metabolized, leaving hypotonic water that shifts into cells.
(Choice C)
Lactated Ringer solution
Lactated Ringer solution is the preferred crystalloid for burn resuscitation as it is isotonic, balanced, and contains lactate, which is metabolized to bicarbonate, helping to buffer acidosis commonly seen in burn patients.
(Choice D)
0.45% Sodium chloride
Half-normal saline is hypotonic and can exacerbate electrolyte imbalances and cause cerebral edema in the setting of rapid infusion for hypovolemic shock.
(Choice E)
0.9% Sodium chloride
Normal saline can cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to its high chloride content (154 mEq/L), making it less ideal for large-volume resuscitation in burn patients who are already prone to acid-base disturbances. The supraphysiologic chloride concentration overwhelms the kidney's ability to excrete excess chloride during massive fluid resuscitation.

pages.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with recurring episodes of lower abdominal pain and bloody stools over a two-month period. She reports having no appetite and has lost eight pounds unintentionally. The patient has a medical history of untreated HIV, with her last known CD4 count at 45 cells/μL. Her stool tests are normal. A colonoscopy reveals ulcerations in the colon, and histopathology detects large cells with distinct intranuclear eosinophilic and intracytoplasmic basophilic inclusions. What is the most probable cause of this patient's symptoms?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
CMV colitis should be suspected in HIV patients with CD4 counts <50 cells/μL who present with bloody diarrhea and characteristic histopathologic findings (large cells with eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions). Normal stool studies are common, making tissue diagnosis via colonoscopy with biopsy essential. Prompt antiviral treatment with ganciclovir or foscarnet is indicated to prevent life-threatening complications.
(Choice A)
Cryptosporidium
Cryptosporidium infection typically causes profuse watery diarrhea without blood in HIV patients and is diagnosed by identifying oocysts in stool samples. Colonic biopsy would not show the large cells with characteristic intranuclear inclusions described in this case.
(Choice B)
Entamoeba histolytica infection
Entamoeba histolytica causes bloody diarrhea with 'flask-shaped' ulcers visible on biopsy, but trophozoites are typically identified in stool samples, which is not the case here.
(Choice C)
Kaposi sarcoma
Gastrointestinal Kaposi sarcoma can occur in HIV patients but typically presents as violaceous nodular lesions on endoscopy rather than ulcerations. It does not cause the characteristic large cells with intranuclear and intracytoplasmic inclusions seen in this case.
(Choice D)
Mycobacterium avium complex
Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) typically causes chronic watery diarrhea and malabsorption in HIV patients with CD4 <50 cells/μL. Diagnosis requires identification of acid-fast bacilli on tissue biopsy or positive cultures, not the large cells with characteristic viral inclusions described here.
(Choice E)
Cytomegalovirus
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis is indicated by large cells with eosinophilic intranuclear and basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions ('owl's eye' appearance) on histopathology. This presentation is classic in severely immunocompromised HIV patients with CD4 counts <50 cells/μL. Treatment involves ganciclovir or foscarnet if ganciclovir resistance is suspected.

pages.question:
A 62-year-old man presents to the emergency department after falling from a ladder while cleaning gutters, approximately 8 feet high, landing on his left side. He reports persistent left flank pain and mild shortness of breath. Vital signs are blood pressure 105/65 mmHg, heart rate 95 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Physical examination reveals tenderness and bruising over the left flank and lower ribs, but no peritoneal signs. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) exam is negative for free fluid. Laboratory studies are shown below. Given the mechanism of injury and clinical findings, what is the most appropriate next step in management?



Hemoglobin	12.5 g/dL
Hematocrit	38 %
White Blood Cell Count	7.2 10^3/μL
Platelet Count	240 10^3/μL
Mean Corpuscular Volume	90 fL
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin	30 pg
Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration	33 g/dL
Red Cell Distribution Width	13 %
Serum Creatinine	0.9 mg/dL
Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)	14 mg/dL
Estimated GFR (eGFR)	95 mL/min/1.73 m²
Sodium	140 mEq/L
Potassium	4.2 mEq/L
Chloride	103 mEq/L
Bicarbonate (HCO3-)	24 mEq/L

answers.text:
Obtain contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
(67.53%)

Perform serial abdominal examinations and observation
(6.49%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with blunt abdominal trauma from a significant fall (8 feet) with clinical findings suggestive of possible splenic injury: left flank pain, tenderness, and bruising. Despite hemodynamic stability and negative FAST exam, the high-risk mechanism and clinical suspicion warrant advanced imaging. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen is the standard of care for hemodynamically stable patients with suspected intra-abdominal injury, providing detailed evaluation of solid organs and detection of active bleeding. Serial observation would be inappropriate given the high clinical suspicion. Other options like chest X-ray, diagnostic peritoneal lavage, immediate surgery, or repeat FAST are either inadequate for abdominal evaluation or not indicated in stable patients.
(Choice A)
Obtain contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen
This is the most appropriate next step for a hemodynamically stable patient with high suspicion for intraabdominal injury despite a negative FAST, as CT provides detailed evaluation of solid organ injuries like splenic laceration. The question has been asked isn't blood and contrast the same contrast color ("white") on CT? Blood and IV contrast are NOT both "white" in a way that makes them indistinguishable: Native blood (extravasated from injury) appears hyperdense (bright) on non-contrast CT due to its high attenuation (typically 40–70 HU for acute hematoma). IV iodinated contrast enhances vascular structures and perfused parenchyma during the arterial/portal venous phase, appearing very hyperdense (200–500+ HU). On contrast-enhanced CT, active bleeding shows as a focal blush or extravasation of contrast — a high-density jet or pool that increases in size on delayed phases — which is readily distinguishable from static hematoma.
(Choice B)
Perform serial abdominal examinations and observation
While serial examinations may be appropriate for very low-suspicion cases, this patient has high clinical suspicion for intra-abdominal injury based on mechanism (8-foot fall), symptoms (persistent flank pain), and physical findings (flank tenderness and bruising). Serial observation alone would delay diagnosis and could miss evolving splenic injury that may require intervention.
(Choice C)
Perform diagnostic peritoneal lavage
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) is largely obsolete in modern trauma care. While it can detect intraperitoneal bleeding, it cannot localize the source of bleeding, has lower specificity than CT, and may give false negatives in retroperitoneal injuries. CT imaging provides superior anatomical detail and is the current standard of care.
(Choice D)
Repeat FAST examination
Repeating FAST is not necessary as it was already negative, and it has limited sensitivity for retroperitoneal or contained injuries; CT is superior for definitive evaluation.
(Choice E)
Obtain chest radiograph
While a chest radiograph would be appropriate to evaluate for rib fractures or pneumothorax given the mechanism and chest pain, it does not provide adequate evaluation of the abdomen or retroperitoneum where splenic injury is suspected. The clinical priority is ruling out intra-abdominal injury.

pages.question: A 4-year-old girl is brought to the urgent care clinic after developing a sudden onset of a seal-like cough and noisy breathing during a family camping trip. She had been exposed to campfire smoke the previous evening and had a runny nose for the past few days. Her parents report that her symptoms worsen when she becomes excited or upset, such as during playtime. Physical examination reveals mild intercostal retractions and inspiratory stridor that improves when she is calm. Her oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, and she is afebrile. What is the most likely pathophysiologic mechanism responsible for this patient's symptoms?

answers.text:
Thick purulent secretions occluding the trachea
(3.23%)

Foreign body obstruction in the distal bronchi
(1.61%)

Edema and narrowing of the proximal trachea
(53.23%)

Swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures
(22.58%)

Bronchospasm with hyperinflation of the lungs
(19.35%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's presentation is consistent with viral croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), which causes subglottic edema and airway narrowing, leading to the characteristic barky cough and inspiratory stridor that worsens with agitation. Croup is most common in children 6 months to 6 years old and typically follows a mild upper respiratory infection.
(Choice A)
Thick purulent secretions occluding the trachea
This describes bacterial tracheitis, which typically presents as a progression from viral croup with high fever, toxic appearance, and thick purulent secretions. Unlike viral croup, bacterial tracheitis requires aggressive airway management and antibiotic therapy due to the severity of illness.
(Choice B)
Foreign body obstruction in the distal bronchi
Foreign body aspiration typically presents with sudden onset choking, unilateral wheezing, or asymmetric breath sounds rather than the bilateral inspiratory stridor and barky cough characteristic of croup. Foreign body obstruction also does not typically worsen with agitation in the pattern seen here.
(Choice C)
Edema and narrowing of the proximal trachea
This is the primary pathophysiologic mechanism in croup, where viral infection leads to inflammation and edema in the subglottic region (below the vocal cords), causing airway narrowing and the characteristic barky cough and stridor. The subglottic area is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway, making even small amounts of edema clinically significant.
(Choice D)
Swelling of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures
This describes epiglottitis, which presents with high fever, drooling, muffled voice, and severe respiratory distress with the patient preferring to sit upright and lean forward (tripod position). Unlike croup, epiglottitis does not cause a barky cough and symptoms do not fluctuate with agitation.
(Choice E)
Bronchospasm with hyperinflation of the lungs
This describes the mechanism in asthma exacerbations, which typically present with expiratory wheezing, prolonged expiration, and chest tightness rather than the inspiratory stridor characteristic of upper airway obstruction. Asthma also rarely causes the distinctive barky cough seen in croup.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old primigravida woman presents with persistent heavy vaginal bleeding 45 minutes after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery of a healthy infant at 39 weeks' gestation. Her pregnancy was complicated by gestational hypertension, for which she was treated with methyldopa. Postpartum, her blood pressure is 152/96 mmHg. On examination, the uterine fundus is soft and boggy at the level of the umbilicus. Bimanual uterine massage is performed, and intravenous oxytocin is initiated, but the bleeding continues. The patient has no history of asthma,Laboratory results are shown below. Which of the following medications is contraindicated in this patient?



WBC	7.2x10^3/µL
RBC	4.8x10^6/µL
Hemoglobin	14.2g/dL
Hematocrit	42.5%
MCV	88fL
MCH	29.6pg
MCHC	33.5g/dL
RDW	13.2%
Platelets	260x10^3/µL
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	6%
Eosinophils	3%
Basophils	1%
Prothrombin Time (PT)	11.8sec
INR	1.0
Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT)	30sec
Fibrinogen	320mg/dL	(normal:200-400mg/dL)
D-Dimer	0.3mg/L
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient has postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony, characterized by heavy vaginal bleeding and a soft, boggy uterus that fails to respond to initial oxytocin therapy. Methylergonovine is contraindicated in patients with hypertensive disorders (including gestational hypertension) due to its potent vasoconstrictive properties that can cause severe hypertension, stroke, or other vascular complications. Carboprost tromethamine is contraindicated in patients with asthma due to bronchospasm risk. Tranexamic acid should be used with caution in patients with active thrombotic disorders, but this patient's normal coagulation profile makes it safe to use. Misoprostol and oxytocin have no specific contraindications in this scenario.
(Choice A)
Oxytocin
Oxytocin is the first-line medication for uterine atony and postpartum hemorrhage. It has no absolute contraindications in patients with hypertension. The patient is already receiving intravenous oxytocin as mentioned in the case, demonstrating its safety in this clinical scenario.
(Choice B)
Carboprost tromethamine
Carboprost tromethamine is a prostaglandin F2α analog used for postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony. It is contraindicated in patients with active asthma or reactive airway disease due to the risk of severe bronchospasm. This patient has no history of asthma, so carboprost would not be contraindicated.
(Choice C)
Tranexamic acid
Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic agent that reduces bleeding by inhibiting fibrinolysis. While it should be used with caution in patients with active thrombotic disorders, this patient's normal coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) indicate no contraindication to its use.
(Choice D)
Methylergonovine
Methylergonovine is an ergot alkaloid that causes uterine contraction but is contraindicated in patients with hypertension due to the risk of exacerbating hypertension and causing stroke or other vascular complications. This patient's gestational hypertension makes it the contraindicated choice.
(Choice E)
Misoprostol
Misoprostol is a prostaglandin E1 analog that causes uterine contractions and can be used rectally or sublingually for postpartum hemorrhage due to atony. It has minimal contraindications and can be safely used in patients with hypertension.

pages.question:
A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her roommate due to increasingly erratic behavior over the past 3 days. The patient has been talking to herself, claiming that her deceased sister is communicating with her through the walls, and insisting that government agents are spying on her to steal her thoughts. She has been disorganized, pacing around the apartment, and refusing to eat, believing her food is poisoned. Two weeks ago, the patient's sister died unexpectedly in a hiking accident, which deeply affected her. The patient has no prior psychiatric history, and her roommate reports that she was functioning normally until shortly after the funeral. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination is unremarkable. Mental status examination reveals disorganized speech, paranoid delusions, and auditory hallucinations. Urine toxicology results are shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?  



Amphetamines	Negative
Barbiturates	Negative
Benzodiazepines	Negative
Cocaine	Negative
Opiates	Negative
Phencyclidine (PCP)	Negative
THC (Cannabinoids)	Negative
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient presents with acute onset of psychotic symptoms including disorganized speech, paranoid delusions, and auditory hallucinations following the traumatic loss of her sister, consistent with brief psychotic disorder. Symptoms have lasted less than 1 month and were triggered by a significant stressor. Other differentials like schizophreniform disorder require longer duration, while acute stress disorder lacks psychotic features, and normal grief does not involve psychosis.
(Choice A)
Persistent complex bereavement disorder
Persistent complex bereavement disorder involves prolonged, intense grief symptoms lasting over 12 months after loss, with significant functional impairment. It does not include psychotic features such as delusions or hallucinations.
(Choice B)
Schizophreniform disorder
Schizophreniform disorder requires psychotic symptoms lasting 1-6 months, which exceeds the duration seen here.
(Choice C)
Delusional disorder
Delusional disorder involves fixed delusions lasting at least 1 month with relatively intact functioning and absence of other significant psychotic symptoms. This patient has prominent hallucinations and disorganized behavior, which are inconsistent with delusional disorder.
(Choice D)
Normal grief reaction
Normal grief involves sadness and mourning but does not include psychotic symptoms like delusions or hallucinations.
(Choice E)
Brief psychotic disorder
Brief psychotic disorder fits with the acute onset of psychotic symptoms lasting less than 1 month, triggered by a significant stressor such as the death of a loved one.

pages.question: A 7-day-old infant is brought in by their parents after experiencing multiple episodes of spitting up and blood-streaked stools. The infant is exclusively breastfed. The family history is notable for both parents having allergic rhinitis and eczema. Vital signs display no abnormalities. On examination, the infant shows satisfactory weight gain and normal hydration status. A stool examination reveals red blood cells and eosinophils. What is the most plausible diagnosis for this condition?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The presence of blood-streaked stools and eosinophils in a young breastfed infant, along with a family history of atopic conditions, suggests cow's milk protein intolerance. This condition arises from dietary proteins found in breast milk after the mother consumes cow's milk, leading to hypersensitivity reactions in some infants.
(Choice A)
Cow's milk protein intolerance
Cow's milk protein intolerance presents with blood-streaked stools and is associated with eosinophils in stool samples. This hypersensitivity can occur in breastfed infants if the mother's diet includes cow's milk.
(Choice B)
Cystic Fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis typically presents with meconium ileus, failure to thrive, and bulky, greasy stools due to pancreatic insufficiency. It does not cause bloody stools or stool eosinophilia.
(Choice C)
Neutropenic enterocolitis
Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) occurs in immunocompromised patients with severe neutropenia, presenting with fever, right lower quadrant pain, and bloody diarrhea. It would not occur in an otherwise healthy neonate.
(Choice D)
Intestinal atresia
Intestinal atresia presents within hours of birth with bilious vomiting, abdominal distension, and failure to pass meconium, not blood-streaked stools with normal feeding tolerance and weight gain.
(Choice E)
Lactose intolerance
Primary lactose intolerance is extremely rare in neonates since lactase activity is normally high at birth. It causes watery diarrhea, not bloody stools or eosinophilia.

pages.question: A 42-year-old man presents to the clinic with a 3-week history of progressive pain in his left lower leg. He recently began training for his first half-marathon after years of a sedentary lifestyle, running 5-6 days per week without gradual buildup. The pain is localized to the mid-shin, worsens with running or walking, and improves with rest. He denies any trauma, fever, or systemic symptoms. On examination, there is point tenderness over the posteromedial tibial border, mild swelling without erythema, and no neurological deficits. A plain radiograph of the tibia is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient has subacute, activity-related leg pain with point tenderness and normal initial X-rays, consistent with a tibial stress fracture due to sudden increase in physical activity. Risk factors include rapid escalation of exercise in previously sedentary individuals.
(Choice A)
Medial tibial stress syndrome
Medial tibial stress syndrome typically presents with diffuse pain along the posteromedial border rather than focal point tenderness. While both conditions can occur with sudden activity increases, the specific point tenderness over the tibial border in this case is more characteristic of stress fracture.
(Choice B)
Osteomyelitis
Osteomyelitis typically presents with fever, erythema, warmth, and systemic symptoms. The subacute timeline, normal vital signs, and absence of infectious signs make this diagnosis unlikely. Plain radiographs may be normal early in osteomyelitis, but the clinical presentation here lacks typical infectious features.
(Choice C)
Stress fracture
This is the most likely diagnosis given the subacute onset of localized, activity-related pain with point tenderness over the tibia in the context of sudden increase in repetitive loading activity, with normal initial X-rays, which is characteristic of stress fractures.
(Choice D)
Deep vein thrombosis
This would typically present with unilateral swelling, warmth, and pain, often without activity relation, and risk factors like immobility; the absence of these and normal exam findings make it unlikely.
(Choice E)
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome
Chronic exertional compartment syndrome typically presents with tight, cramping pain during exercise that resolves quickly with rest, often with paresthesias or weakness. The focal point tenderness and swelling seen here are not characteristic of compartment syndrome.

pages.question:
A 38-year-old female comes to the clinic with complaints of feeling persistently tired and weak over the last several months. She reports no recent menstruation due to a prior hysterectomy. She denies smoking, alcohol consumption, or any significant previous medical issues. Her blood pressure is measured at 118/76 mmHg, and her pulse is 80 beats per minute. Physical examination reveals no notable findings. Laboratory tests are as follows:

Hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL
MCV 74 fL
MCHC 29%
White blood cell count 7,500/mm3
ESR 12 mm/hr

Both serum iron and ferritin measurements are reduced. What is the most appropriate initial step in the management of this patient?

answers.text:
Conduct a fecal occult blood test
(48.92%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient is likely affected by iron-deficiency anemia, characterized by lower hemoglobin levels, reduced mean corpuscular volume (MCV), and decreased serum iron and ferritin. In adults, especially those not menstruating, this condition often signals chronic blood loss, typically from the gastrointestinal tract. The initial management focuses on detecting occult bleeding, often via a fecal occult blood test, which may reveal underlying gastrointestinal pathologies like polyps, ulcers, or other conditions causing blood loss.
(Choice A)
Evaluate for celiac disease
While celiac disease can cause iron deficiency through malabsorption, gastrointestinal blood loss is a much more common cause in non-menstruating adults. Celiac evaluation would be considered if initial workup for bleeding sources is negative.
(Choice B)
Implement a high-iron diet
Dietary iron deficiency is rare in developed countries and unlikely to cause severe iron deficiency anemia in adults. Even with dietary modifications, this degree of anemia suggests pathologic blood loss that must be investigated.
(Choice C)
Order an erythropoietin level
Erythropoietin levels are typically elevated in iron deficiency anemia as the kidneys respond appropriately to anemia. This test is more useful in evaluating anemia of chronic disease or chronic kidney disease, not iron deficiency.
(Choice D)
Conduct a fecal occult blood test
In the case of iron deficiency anemia in adult females (non-menstruating) or males, investigating gastrointestinal blood loss through a fecal occult blood test is essential.
(Choice E)
Commence iron supplementation
While iron supplementation will eventually be needed to correct the anemia, starting treatment before identifying the underlying cause of iron loss could mask ongoing bleeding and delay diagnosis of potentially serious conditions like colorectal cancer or peptic ulcer disease.

pages.question:
A 68-year-old African American woman reports frequent episodes of her vision dimming and weakness in her left arm that lasts about 10 minutes since the past month. Her medical history includes long-standing hypertension, controlled type 2 diabetes, and high cholesterol. She has been smoking half a pack of cigarettes daily for 30 years. Her family history is positive for coronary artery disease. Her current medications are lisinopril, metformin, and atorvastatin. On examination, her blood pressure reads 165/100 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, respirations are 18/min, and temperature is 37C (98.6F). Laboratory findings show:

 Fasting blood glucose: 190 mg/dL
 Total cholesterol: 250 mg/dL
 LDL cholesterol: 140 mg/dL
 HDL cholesterol: 60 mg/dL

What is the primary risk factor contributing to her transient ischemic attacks?

answers.text:
Family history of coronary artery disease
(1.14%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
In this clinical context, the patient's poorly controlled hypertension (165/100 mmHg) emerges as the strongest risk factor for her transient ischemic attacks. Hypertension is the most important modifiable risk factor for stroke, with elevated blood pressure causing endothelial damage, accelerating atherosclerosis, and promoting thrombosis. While this patient has multiple cardiovascular risk factors (diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking), her markedly elevated blood pressure represents the most immediate target for stroke prevention. Aggressive blood pressure management should be the primary therapeutic priority to reduce her cerebrovascular risk.
(Choice A)
Family history of coronary artery disease
Family history plays a role in cardiovascular risks but is less significant than direct physiological factors like hypertension.
(Choice B)
Hypertension
Hypertension is a prevalent risk factor that significantly elevates the risk of stroke, including transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), due to its effect on blood vessel walls, increasing the likelihood of atherosclerosis and occlusion.
(Choice C)
Smoking
While smoking significantly increases stroke risk through endothelial dysfunction and accelerated atherosclerosis, hypertension has a stronger direct impact on cerebrovascular events and is the most modifiable risk factor in this patient with markedly elevated blood pressure (165/100 mmHg).
(Choice D)
Hypercholesterolemia
Hypercholesterolemia contributes to atherosclerotic plaque formation and stroke risk, particularly with this patient's elevated LDL (140 mg/dL). However, hypertension has a more direct and immediate impact on cerebrovascular events, especially given her markedly elevated blood pressure reading.
(Choice E)
Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus significantly increases stroke risk through accelerated atherosclerosis and endothelial dysfunction, and this patient has poor glycemic control (fasting glucose 190 mg/dL). However, hypertension remains the strongest modifiable risk factor for TIA/stroke, particularly with her severely elevated blood pressure (165/100 mmHg).

pages.question: A 19-year-old nulliparous college student presents to the student health clinic 60 hours after having unprotected sexual intercourse during a weekend trip. She reports no prior history of sexually transmitted infections and is not currently using any form of contraception. Her last menstrual period was 12 days ago, and she is concerned about the risk of unintended pregnancy. She inquires about the most effective method of emergency contraception that can be initiated at this time. Which of the following options is the most effective for preventing pregnancy in this scenario?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The copper-containing intrauterine device is the most effective method of emergency contraception, with efficacy exceeding 99% when inserted within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse. It primarily works by impairing sperm motility and preventing fertilization or implantation. Levonorgestrel and ulipristal are oral options that delay ovulation but are less effective, particularly if ovulation is imminent. Combined oral contraceptives can be used as emergency contraception but have lower efficacy and more side effects. Depot medroxyprogesterone is a long-acting contraceptive but does not serve as emergency contraception and would not prevent pregnancy if conception has already occurred.
(Choice A)
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate injection
Depot medroxyprogesterone is a long-term contraceptive method but is not indicated for emergency contraception; it does not prevent pregnancy if ovulation or fertilization has already occurred and takes time to become effective.
(Choice B)
Copper-containing intrauterine device
The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception method, with over 99% efficacy when inserted within 120 hours of unprotected intercourse; it impairs fertilization and implantation and provides ongoing contraception.
(Choice C)
Levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive pill
Levonorgestrel is an effective oral emergency contraceptive that delays ovulation but has lower efficacy (approximately 85%) compared to the copper IUD. Its effectiveness decreases significantly after 72 hours post-intercourse, making it less optimal at 60 hours when ovulation may be imminent.
(Choice D)
Ulipristal acetate pill
Ulipristal acetate is a selective progesterone receptor modulator that delays ovulation and maintains effectiveness up to 120 hours post-intercourse with approximately 85% efficacy. While more effective than levonorgestrel at this timeframe, it still has lower efficacy than the copper IUD and requires a prescription.
(Choice E)
Combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pills
Combined oral contraceptives can be used in a high-dose regimen for emergency contraception (Yuzpe method), but they have significantly lower efficacy (approximately 75%) and are associated with substantial nausea and vomiting. This method is rarely used today given better alternatives.

pages.question: A 27-year-old construction worker is brought to the ER after a high fall from a scaffold. His protective helmet is in place but there's noticeable impact damage to it. Upon arrival, he is drowsy and difficult to rouse. Initial vital signs show a blood pressure of 75/40 mmHg and a heart rate of 138 beats per minute. His lung fields are clear, but there is bruising over the lower chest and upper abdomen. The abdomen is tender and mildly distended, with minimal bowel sounds. His neck veins appear flat. After administration of two liters of IV fluids, his blood pressure marginally improves to 82/45 mmHg. A focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST) reveals free fluid in the abdominal cavity but no clear indication of solid organ laceration. What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?

answers.text: Hemodialysis removes albumin from the circulation during each session, causing a post-dialysis albumin nadir that does not reflect true nutritional status
Chronic uremic inflammation suppresses hepatic albumin synthesis as a negative acute phase reactant, causing albumin to fall independent of actual protein nutritional status
Impaired renal catabolism of albumin in chronic kidney disease causes abnormal albumin accumulation, artificially elevating serum levels and masking protein depletion
Metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease accelerates hepatic albumin degradation, causing albumin to fall regardless of dietary protein intake
Erythropoietin therapy in hemodialysis patients competitively inhibits hepatic albumin synthesis by diverting amino acid precursors toward hemoglobin production

pages.explanation:
Explanation
In trauma patients with hemodynamic instability despite adequate fluid resuscitation and positive FAST exam showing intraperitoneal fluid, urgent laparotomy is indicated for hemorrhage control. The combination of hypotension, tachycardia, abdominal tenderness with free fluid, and poor response to fluids suggests ongoing intra-abdominal bleeding requiring immediate surgical intervention.
(Choice A)
Retrograde Urethrogram
Retrograde urethrogram is used to evaluate urethral injury, typically when there's blood at the urethral meatus, scrotal hematoma, or high-riding prostate. This patient's presentation suggests intra-abdominal hemorrhage, not urethral trauma, making this study irrelevant.
(Choice B)
Thoracostomy Tube Placement
Thoracostomy tube placement treats pneumothorax or hemothorax. This patient has clear lung fields and normal chest examination findings. The hemodynamic instability is due to intra-abdominal bleeding, not thoracic injury.
(Choice C)
Urgent Laparotomy
Given the patient's hemodynamic instability and suspicion of intra-abdominal hemorrhage, urgent laparotomy is warranted to control the bleeding.
(Choice D)
Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography
ERCP is a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure for biliopancreatic disorders, typically performed electively. It has no role in the acute management of trauma patients with hemodynamic instability and suspected intra-abdominal hemorrhage.
(Choice E)
Abdominal MRI
MRI takes too long to perform and requires a stable patient who can remain motionless. In hemodynamically unstable trauma patients requiring immediate intervention, MRI would delay life-saving treatment and is contraindicated.

pages.question: A 48-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis three times per week presents for a routine clinic visit. Her nephrologist is concerned about her nutritional status. She reports eating one to two meals per day with poor appetite. Her weight has been stable at 132 lbs with a height of 5'4' (BMI 22.7 kg/m²). On examination, there is mild temporal wasting and decreased interosseous muscle bulk. Her mid-arm muscle circumference is at the 12th percentile. Laboratory studies show albumin 3.2 g/dL, prealbumin 18 mg/dL, transferrin 195 mg/dL, total lymphocyte count 1,050/mm³, and C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (elevated). The dietitian notes that the standard laboratory markers may be difficult to interpret in this patient. Which of the following best explains why albumin is a less reliable marker of nutritional status in this patient compared to a patient without chronic kidney disease?

answers.text:
Hemodialysis removes albumin from the circulation during each session, causing a post-dialysis albumin nadir that does not reflect true nutritional status
(0%)

Chronic uremic inflammation suppresses hepatic albumin synthesis as a negative acute phase reactant, causing albumin to fall independent of actual protein nutritional status
(0%)

Impaired renal catabolism of albumin in chronic kidney disease causes abnormal albumin accumulation, artificially elevating serum levels and masking protein depletion
(0%)

Metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease accelerates hepatic albumin degradation, causing albumin to fall regardless of dietary protein intake
(0%)

Erythropoietin therapy in hemodialysis patients competitively inhibits hepatic albumin synthesis by diverting amino acid precursors toward hemoglobin production
(0%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
In hemodialysis patients, albumin is confounded by multiple non-nutritional factors, primarily chronic uremic inflammation which suppresses albumin synthesis as a negative acute phase reactant (evidenced by elevated CRP). Additional confounders include volume overload diluting serum albumin and minimal albumin losses into dialysate. These factors cause albumin to underestimate true nutritional status, making anthropometric measures (such as mid-arm muscle circumference) and alternative markers like prealbumin more reliable for nutritional assessment in this population.
(Choice A)
Hemodialysis removes albumin from the circulation during each session, causing a post-dialysis albumin nadir that does not reflect true nutritional status
Standard hemodialysis membranes do not remove significant amounts of albumin due to its large molecular weight of approximately 66,000 daltons. While minimal albumin losses into dialysate do occur during each session, these losses are small and clinically insignificant. The primary reasons albumin is unreliable as a nutritional marker in hemodialysis patients are chronic inflammation suppressing albumin synthesis as a negative acute phase reactant and volume distribution effects, not dialytic albumin removal.
(Choice B)
Chronic uremic inflammation suppresses hepatic albumin synthesis as a negative acute phase reactant, causing albumin to fall independent of actual protein nutritional status
Albumin is a negative acute phase reactant — its hepatic synthesis is actively suppressed by pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha, which redirect hepatic synthetic capacity toward positive acute phase proteins such as CRP, fibrinogen, and ferritin. In hemodialysis patients, chronic low-grade uremic inflammation is nearly universal, as evidenced by this patient's elevated CRP of 18 mg/L. This chronic inflammatory state suppresses albumin synthesis, causing serum albumin to fall independent of actual dietary protein intake or body protein stores. Additionally, hemodialysis patients may have volume overload diluting serum albumin, and some albumin is lost into the dialysate during each session. These confounders mean that a hemodialysis patient's albumin may be low due to inflammation and volume distribution rather than protein malnutrition, or conversely, adequate nutritional status may be masked by inflammation-driven suppression. Anthropometric measures (mid-arm muscle circumference, temporal wasting) and diet history provide more direct and less confounded assessments of nutritional status in this population.
(Choice C)
Impaired renal catabolism of albumin in chronic kidney disease causes abnormal albumin accumulation, artificially elevating serum levels and masking protein depletion
The kidney is a site of albumin catabolism, and in advanced CKD, reduced renal albumin catabolism could theoretically contribute to maintaining albumin levels. However, in hemodialysis patients, the predominant effects are downward pressure on albumin from chronic uremic inflammation (suppressing synthesis as a negative acute phase reactant) and volume distribution changes. Albumin levels in dialysis patients are typically low or low-normal rather than elevated, making this mechanism clinically irrelevant compared to inflammatory suppression.
(Choice D)
Metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease accelerates hepatic albumin degradation, causing albumin to fall regardless of dietary protein intake
Metabolic acidosis in CKD does promote protein catabolism, particularly skeletal muscle protein breakdown, contributing to sarcopenia. However, albumin degradation is not the primary mechanism by which metabolic acidosis affects serum albumin. The dominant reason albumin is unreliable as a nutritional marker in hemodialysis patients is its behavior as a negative acute phase reactant in the setting of chronic uremic inflammation, not metabolic acidosis-driven hepatic albumin degradation.
(Choice E)
Erythropoietin therapy in hemodialysis patients competitively inhibits hepatic albumin synthesis by diverting amino acid precursors toward hemoglobin production
Erythropoietin-stimulating agents used in hemodialysis patients stimulate erythropoiesis and hemoglobin synthesis but do not competitively inhibit hepatic albumin synthesis to a clinically significant degree. The liver has substantial synthetic capacity and can produce both albumin and acute phase proteins simultaneously. The primary reason albumin is unreliable as a nutritional marker in dialysis patients remains its suppression by chronic uremic inflammation as a negative acute phase reactant.

pages.question: A 28-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive numbness and tingling in his shoulders and arms, extending down to his hands. He reports difficulty gripping objects and buttoning his shirt, but his leg strength remains normal. On examination, he has decreased sensation to pinprick and temperature over the upper back, shoulders, and arms in a bilateral cape-like distribution, while vibration and position sense are intact throughout. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the bilateral upper extremities and 5/5 in the lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 2+ in all extremities. MRI of the spine is ordered. What is the most likely finding on imaging that explains his symptoms?

pages.question: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with sudden-onset coughing, wheezing, and difficulty breathing that began during his birthday party. The parents report that he was eating cake and playing with popped balloon fragments shortly before the symptoms started. On examination, the child is in moderate respiratory distress with decreased breath sounds over the left lung field. A chest x-ray reveals hyperinflation of the left lung with mediastinal shift to the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's sudden-onset respiratory distress with unilateral hyperinflation and mediastinal shift on x-ray are indicative of foreign body aspiration, most common in young children. Clinical features include acute cough, dyspnea, and asymmetric breath sounds. Rigid bronchoscopy is the preferred method for diagnosis and removal of the aspirated object in children. Other options are inappropriate as they treat alternative diagnoses like asthma, infection, or mucus plugging without addressing the foreign body.
(Choice A)
Nebulized albuterol
Nebulized albuterol treats bronchospasm in conditions like asthma or reactive airway disease but does not address the underlying mechanical obstruction from an aspirated foreign body.
(Choice B)
Flexible bronchoscopy
Flexible bronchoscopy can visualize the foreign body but has limited ability to remove objects in pediatric patients due to smaller working channel and less rigid suction capabilities compared to rigid bronchoscopy.
(Choice C)
Rigid bronchoscopy
Rigid bronchoscopy is the gold standard for both diagnosis and removal of aspirated foreign bodies in children, allowing for airway control and extraction.
(Choice D)
Chest physiotherapy
Chest physiotherapy helps mobilize secretions in conditions like cystic fibrosis or pneumonia but cannot dislodge a solid foreign body causing complete or partial airway obstruction.
(Choice E)
Oral amoxicillin
Oral antibiotics like amoxicillin treat bacterial pneumonia but are not indicated for foreign body aspiration, which is a mechanical problem requiring physical removal.

pages.question: A 42-year-old Japanese female visits her primary care physician for sudden, severe headaches that have been disturbing her sleep over the past three weeks. She describes the pain as sharp, intense, and localized behind her left eye, often radiating to her forehead and temple. These episodes last about an hour, occurring at least once every night. She notes tearing in her left eye, nasal congestion, and occasional drooping of her eyelid during these episodes. She suffered a similar bout two years ago that lasted several weeks. Which of the following is the most effective treatment for halting her headache during these acute episodes?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
The patient's symptoms are indicative of cluster headaches, characterized by intense pain, lacrimation, nasal congestion, and Horner's syndrome. Oxygen therapy at 100% works by inducing vasoconstriction in dilated cranial vessels, thus providing quick relief and is considered first-line in instant abortive therapy for cluster headaches.
(Choice A)
100% oxygen
Inhalation of 100% oxygen for 15 minutes is the most rapid and highly effective abortive treatment for acute cluster headache attacks.
(Choice B)
Lithium
Lithium is used as a preventive treatment for cluster headaches, particularly for chronic cluster headaches. However, it has no role in aborting acute attacks as it requires steady-state levels to be effective and works through long-term mechanisms.
(Choice C)
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulator
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS) has shown efficacy in cluster headache treatment and is FDA-approved for this indication. However, it typically takes longer to provide relief compared to 100% oxygen inhalation and is generally considered a second-line abortive option.
(Choice D)
Nasal sumatriptan
Subcutaneous sumatriptan is highly effective for aborting cluster headaches and works faster than the nasal formulation. However, 100% oxygen remains the preferred first-line abortive treatment due to its rapid onset (often within 15 minutes), lack of medication limits, and excellent safety profile.
(Choice E)
Oral NSAIDs
While NSAIDs may provide some analgesic effect, they are too slow-acting to effectively abort acute cluster headache attacks. Cluster headaches require rapid-onset treatments due to the severe, time-limited nature of the pain.

pages.question: A father brings his son to the pediatric office for a check-up. During the assessment, the child demonstrates that he can walk unaided, uses two distinct words, tosses various items, and responds when his name is called. Based on these behaviors, what is the most plausible age of this child?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
At 12 months, toddlers often reach significant developmental milestones. Physically, they are mobile, showing gross motor skills through independent walking. Cognitively, they start basic verbal communication, showing an ability to use two distinct words. Additionally, social development includes responding to their name, and fine motor skills are exhibited when they throw objects. Recognizing these milestones is crucial in evaluating typical child development and potential delays.
(Choice A)
18 months
At 18 months, children typically run, kick balls, use 10-25 words, and follow simple commands. The basic milestones described (independent walking, two words) emerge earlier at 12 months.
(Choice B)
12 months
A typical 12-month-old can walk alone, uses two words, and throws objects. These milestones align with the age.
(Choice C)
6 months
A 6-month-old typically sits with support, babbles, and transfers objects between hands, but cannot walk independently or use distinct words. Walking typically begins around 12 months.
(Choice D)
9 months
At 9 months, children typically crawl, pull to stand, and may say 'mama' or 'dada' non-specifically, but independent walking and use of two distinct meaningful words are not expected until around 12 months.
(Choice E)
15 months
While a 15-month-old can walk independently and use words, they typically demonstrate more advanced skills like walking backwards, climbing stairs, and using 4-6 words. The described milestones are more consistent with 12 months.

pages.question:
A 38-year-old man undergoes a routine health screening for a new job. He is asymptomatic and denies any history of abdominal pain, jaundice, pruritus, or changes in bowel habits. His past medical history is unremarkable, and he takes no medications. Laboratory values are shown below. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) shows multifocal strictures and segmental dilations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?



Hemoglobin	13.4 g/dL
Hematocrit	40%
Red blood cell count	4.7 x10^6/µL
Mean corpuscular volume	86 fL
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin	29 pg
Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration	33 g/dL
Red cell distribution width	13%
White blood cell count	7800/µL
Neutrophils	60%
Lymphocytes	30%
Monocytes	6%
Eosinophils	3%
Basophils	1%
Platelet count	250000/µL
Alkaline phosphatase	350 U/L
Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase	280 U/L
Total bilirubin	0.9 mg/dL
Aspartate aminotransferase (AST)	32 U/L
Alanine aminotransferase (ALT)	30 U/L
pages.explanation:
Explanation
This patient's asymptomatic presentation with cholestatic liver enzyme elevations (high alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase) and MRCP findings of multifocal biliary strictures and dilations are diagnostic of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). PSC has a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), particularly ulcerative colitis. Colonoscopy is recommended at the time of PSC diagnosis to screen for underlying IBD and to establish baseline for colon cancer surveillance, as patients with PSC and IBD have an increased risk of colorectal cancer.
(Choice A)
Ursodeoxycholic acid therapy
Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) has not been shown to improve survival or prevent disease progression in PSC, and current guidelines do not recommend its routine use. Treatment focuses on managing complications and surveillance rather than disease-modifying therapy.
(Choice B)
Abdominal ultrasound
Abdominal ultrasound is less sensitive than MRCP for detecting biliary abnormalities in PSC and is not needed after diagnostic MRCP findings.
(Choice C)
Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy is the most appropriate next step to evaluate for concurrent inflammatory bowel disease, which is present in up to 80% of patients with PSC, and to initiate colon cancer surveillance if IBD is found.
(Choice D)
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with sphincterotomy
ERCP is therapeutic for dominant strictures or complications like cholangitis but is not indicated as the initial step in an asymptomatic patient with diagnostic MRCP.
(Choice E)
Liver biopsy
Liver biopsy is not necessary for diagnosis when MRCP findings are classic for PSC and laboratory values show a cholestatic pattern. Biopsy is reserved for cases with atypical MRCP findings or when fibrosis staging is needed for prognosis.

pages.question: A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to uncontrolled diabetes is admitted to the intensive care unit after a cardiac arrest at home. He has been on hemodialysis for 5 years and has multiple comorbidities, including cardiomyopathy and peripheral vascular disease. Despite aggressive resuscitation, he remains comatose with minimal brainstem reflexes and requires mechanical ventilation and vasopressor support. Imaging shows evidence of anoxic brain injury. The patient's wife and adult children are deeply religious and express strong reluctance to withdraw life-sustaining treatments, citing hopes for a divine miracle. They insist on continuing all possible interventions. The medical team believes further escalation of care, such as initiating continuous renal replacement therapy or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, would be futile given the poor neurological prognosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing this situation?

answers.text:
Escalate care by initiating continuous renal replacement therapy and consulting for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
(2.15%)

Transfer the patient to a long-term acute care facility without further discussion
(2.15%)

Unilaterally withdraw all life-sustaining treatments despite family objections
(5.38%)

Reframe the discussion to explore agreement on no escalation of treatment orders
(80.65%)

Request an urgent ethics committee consultation to override the family's treatment preferences
(9.68%)

pages.explanation:
Explanation
No Escalation of Treatment (NEOT) orders establish predetermined limits on interventions that will not be initiated regardless of clinical deterioration. This approach allows families to maintain hope while setting appropriate medical boundaries. NEOT orders help bridge the gap between family wishes and medical judgment by continuing current supportive care while preventing futile interventions that would not improve outcomes given the patient's poor neurological prognosis.
(Choice A)
Escalate care by initiating continuous renal replacement therapy and consulting for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation
Escalating to aggressive interventions like CRRT and ECMO would be medically inappropriate given the poor neurological prognosis and would constitute futile care that prolongs suffering without meaningful benefit.
(Choice B)
Transfer the patient to a long-term acute care facility without further discussion
This avoids addressing the core issue and does not involve the family in decision-making, potentially escalating conflict.
(Choice C)
Unilaterally withdraw all life-sustaining treatments despite family objections
Unilaterally withdrawing life support without family consensus violates principles of shared decision-making and can lead to legal complications. Healthcare providers should seek agreement through discussion before considering more drastic measures.
(Choice D)
Reframe the discussion to explore agreement on no escalation of treatment orders
NEOT orders allow for maintaining current care while setting limits on further interventions, helping to align with family wishes, reduce futility, and alleviate guilt.
(Choice E)
Request an urgent ethics committee consultation to override the family's treatment preferences
While ethics consultation can be valuable for complex cases, using it as a first step to override family wishes is inappropriate. The primary goal should be facilitating communication and understanding between the medical team and family.

pages.question: A 32-year-old woman with endometriosis is undergoing laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy under general anesthesia. Immediately following CO2 insufflation to establish pneumoperitoneum at 14 mmHg, the patient's heart rate drops from 78 bpm to 42 bpm, and the rhythm on the monitor is shown below. Blood pressure remains stable, and the bradycardia resolves promptly after administration of glycopyrrolate. What is the most likely mechanism underlying this intraoperative bradycardia?
pages.explanation:
Explanation
CO2 insufflation during laparoscopy increases intra-abdominal pressure, which activates peritoneal stretch receptors and stimulates vagal afferents, leading to increased parasympathetic tone and resulting bradycardia. The rapid response to glycopyrrolate (an anticholinergic agent) confirms vagal mediation. Alternative mechanisms like CO2 gas embolism (causing cardiovascular collapse), inadequate anesthesia (causing sympathetic activation), hypercapnia from CO2 absorption (causing sympathetic stimulation), and vena cava compression (causing hypotension without vagal stimulation) do not explain isolated bradycardia responsive to anticholinergics.
(Choice A)
Peritoneal stretching
Increased intra-abdominal pressure from CO2 insufflation stretches peritoneal receptors, stimulating vagal afferents and increasing parasympathetic tone, which causes bradycardia.
(Choice B)
Systemic CO2 absorption causing hypercapnia
Systemic absorption of CO2 during insufflation can cause hypercapnia, which stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and respiratory drive, typically resulting in tachycardia and hypertension. This mechanism would not produce vagally-mediated bradycardia.
(Choice C)
CO2 gas embolism
CO2 gas embolism occurs when CO2 enters the vascular system, typically presenting with acute cardiovascular collapse, hypotension, arrhythmias, and hypoxia due to gas bubbles obstructing circulation. This would not cause isolated bradycardia that responds to anticholinergics.
(Choice D)
Inadequate anesthesia depth
Inadequate anesthesia depth (light anesthesia) triggers sympathetic activation in response to surgical stimulation, typically causing tachycardia, hypertension, and patient movement. This would not cause bradycardia that responds to anticholinergics.
(Choice E)
Vena cava compression
Compression of the inferior vena cava reduces venous return, potentially causing hypotension, but it does not directly lead to vagally mediated bradycardia.

pages.question: A 48-year-old man with a 5-year history of systemic sclerosis presents with worsening dysphagia to both solids and liquids, along with regurgitation of undigested food and nocturnal heartburn. He has a history of Raynaud phenomenon and interstitial lung disease. Physical examination reveals skin tightening on the fingers and face. Barium swallow shows a dilated esophagus with poor motility, and high-resolution manometry demonstrates absent contractility in the distal esophagus and a hypotensive lower esophageal sphincter. What is the primary esophageal pathology causing these motility abnormalities?

answers.text:
Autoimmune destruction of the myenteric plexus
(29.69%)

Excessive collagen deposition in submucosal layers
(0%)

Vascular ischemia of the esophageal wall
(0%)

Chronic mucosal inflammation and stricture formation
(9.38%)
